slots.text: There was once a man who had heard, as a child, that beautiful story of how God tempted Abraham, and how Abraham stood firm in the temptation, kept the faith, and, against all expectation, received a son a second time. As he grew older, he read that same story with even greater admiration; for life had separated what had been united in the child’s pious simplicity. The older he grew, the more often his thoughts turned to that story. His enthusiasm grew stronger and stronger, and yet he could understand the story less and less. At last he forgot everything else over it. His soul had only one wish — to see Abraham — and only one longing: to have been a witness to that event. What he craved was not to see the fair lands of the East, nor the earthly splendor of the land of promise, nor that God-fearing married couple whose old age God blessed, nor the patriarch’s venerable figure, full of years, nor the lush youth of Isaac, the gift of God — he would not have minded if the same thing had taken place on a barren heath. What he yearned for was to go with them on the three-day journey, when Abraham rode with sorrow going ahead of him and Isaac by his side. His wish was to be there in the hour when Abraham raised his eyes and saw Mount Moriah far off, the hour when he left the donkeys behind and climbed the mountain alone with Isaac; for what absorbed him was not the imagination’s artful weaving but the shudder of thought.

That man was not a thinker. He felt no need to get beyond faith. To him it seemed that it must be the most glorious thing of all to be remembered as its father, and an enviable lot to possess it, even if no one knew.
That man was not a learned exegete; he did not know Hebrew. Had he known Hebrew, perhaps he would easily have understood the story of Abraham.
“And God tempted Abraham and said to him: Take Isaac, your only son, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on a mountain that I will show you.”

It was early morning. Abraham rose early, had the donkeys saddled and left his tent, taking Isaac with him; but from the window Sarah followed them with her eyes, down through the valley, until she could no longer see them. For three days they rode in silence. On the morning of the fourth day Abraham still did not say a word, but he raised his eyes and saw Mount Moriah far off. He left the young servants behind and, with Isaac by the hand, went up the mountain alone. But Abraham said to himself: “Still, I will not hide from Isaac where this road is leading him.” He stopped and laid his hand on Isaac’s head to bless him, and Isaac bent down to receive the blessing. And Abraham’s face was fatherliness itself, his look gentle, his words full of admonition. But Isaac could not understand him; his soul could not be lifted up. He threw his arms around Abraham’s knees, he fell pleading at his feet, he begged for his young life, for his bright hopes; he reminded him of the joy in Abraham’s house, he reminded him of the sorrow and the loneliness. Then Abraham lifted the boy to his feet and walked on with him, hand in hand, and his words were full of comfort and admonition. But Isaac could not understand him. Abraham climbed Mount Moriah, but Isaac did not understand him. Then for a moment Abraham turned his face away from him; and when Isaac looked at Abraham’s face a second time, it had changed. His look was wild, his whole figure was horror. He gripped Isaac by the chest, flung him to the ground and said: “Stupid boy, do you believe I am your father? I am an idol-worshipper. Do you believe it is God’s command? No, it is what I want.” Then Isaac trembled and in his anxiety cried out: “God in heaven, have mercy on me! God of Abraham, have mercy on me! If I have no father on earth, be my father yourself!” But Abraham whispered to himself: “Lord in heaven, I thank you. After all, it is better that he believes I am a monster than that he loses his faith in you.”

When the child is to be weaned, the mother blackens her breast; after all, it would be a pity for the breast to look lovely when the child is not allowed to have it. Then the child believes the breast has changed; but the mother, she is the same, and her look is as loving and tender as ever. Happy the one who needed no more terrible means to wean the child!

It was early morning. Abraham rose early; he put his arms around Sarah, the bride of his old age, and Sarah kissed Isaac, who had lifted her shame from her — her pride, her hope through all generations. Then they rode in silence along the road, and Abraham’s eyes were fixed on the ground until the fourth day, when he raised his eyes and saw Mount Moriah a long way off, but his eyes turned again to the ground. Without a word he arranged the wood and bound Isaac; without a word he drew the knife. Then he caught sight of the ram God had provided. That he sacrificed, and went home. — — — From that day on Abraham grew old. He could not forget that God had required this of him. Isaac flourished as before; but Abraham’s eye was darkened, and he saw joy no more.

When the child has grown big and is to be weaned, the mother covers her breast with a maiden’s modesty, and then the child has a mother no more. Happy the child who did not lose its mother in any other way!

It was early morning. Abraham rose early; he kissed Sarah, the young mother, and Sarah kissed Isaac, her delight, her joy for all time. And Abraham rode along the road, lost in thought; he was thinking of Hagar and the son whom he had driven out into the desert. He climbed Mount Moriah; he drew the knife.

It was a still evening. Abraham rode out alone, and he rode to Mount Moriah; he fell on his face and begged God to forgive him his sin — that he had wanted to sacrifice Isaac, that as a father he had forgotten his duty to his son. After that he often rode his lonely way, but he found no peace. He could not grasp that it was a sin to have wanted to sacrifice to God the best thing he possessed — the thing for which he would gladly have laid down his own life many times over. And if it was a sin, if he had not loved Isaac in that way, then he could not understand how it could be forgiven; for what sin was more terrible?

When the child is to be weaned, then the mother is not without sorrow either, because she and the child are drawing further and further apart — that the child who first lay beneath her heart, and later rested at her breast, will no longer be so near. So together they grieve the brief grief. Happy the one who kept the child so near, and did not need to grieve any more!

It was early morning. In Abraham’s house everything had been made ready for the journey. He said goodbye to Sarah, and Eliezer, the faithful servant, accompanied him along the road until Eliezer turned back. Abraham and Isaac rode on together in harmony until they reached Mount Moriah. Calm and gentle, Abraham prepared everything for the sacrifice; but as he turned away and drew the knife, Isaac saw Abraham’s left hand clench in despair and a shiver pass through his whole frame — but Abraham drew the knife.

Then they returned home, and Sarah hastened out to meet them; but Isaac had lost the faith. Not a word about it has ever been said in the world, and Isaac never spoke to anyone about what he had seen, and Abraham never suspected that anyone had seen it.
When the child is to be weaned, the mother has stronger food at hand, so that the child will not perish. Happy the one who has stronger food at hand!

In this way, and in many similar ways, the man of whom we are speaking thought about this event. And every time he came home after a pilgrimage to Mount Moriah, he sank down with weariness, folded his hands and said: “Yet no one was as great as Abraham. Who is able to understand him?”
